newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE-Pow wow a return to Canadian Indian tradition.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Pow wow a return to Canadian Indian tradition.

text.p: Working amid cars and pickup trucks glinting in the evening sun, Lee Sleigh pieced together the brightly colored fabric, beads and feathers of his ceremonial Indian dancing costume.

Sleigh, a soft-spoken 28-year-old from Alberta's Blackfoot Indian Reserve, was transforming himself into an explosion of red, yellow and black to dance at the opening of this year's Buffalo Days Pow Wow at Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump, 109 miles (175 km) south of Calgary.

Taking a break from the laborious process, he said his return to ancient traditions was his salvation from poverty and alcoholism, which have long plagued Canadian Indian youth. "I danced when I was a kid," he said. "I went through my teen years and then I had to explore the fast lane in the city and stuff like that. But I'm glad I'm back."

Last month's event, one of several held each summer in Canada, is special because of its location at the foot of a sandstone cliff where for thousands of years hunters drove buffalo to plummet to their deaths in order to provide Indian families with food and other necessities.

Indian drummers and dancers of all ages from Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan provinces and Montana across the U.S. border gathered for the weekend to compete for prize money and pay homage to their ancestors on a stage surrounded by pine boughs and painted tepees. Alcohol was forbidden.

Organizers from the Peigan Indian Reserve, across a gravel road from the site, said they aimed to keep the pow wow steeped in tradition despite throngs of spectators from around the world. Pow wows historically were celebrations held in the summer after spiritual gatherings.

"At a lot of the pow wows you go to now you see motor homes and you see pup tents. You'll see maybe one or two tepees," Buffalo Days coordinator Louisa Crowshoe said. "Here we try to keep it as traditional as possible."

That is not surprising given the site, which is sacred to the region's native population. Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump, where Alberta prairie meets rolling Rocky Mountain foothills, is one of the last and best-preserved of several buffalo killing cliffs used by Plains Indians for about 5,000 years.

According to local legend, it got its name about 150 years ago when a young brave lowered himself onto a ledge to watch a herd plummet 10 yards (metres) to its demise. The hunt that day was very good and as bodies piled up he became trapped between the buffalo and the cliff. When his people came to butcher the animals, they found him with his skull crushed.

Today, the cliff -- minus the buffalo herds since the late 1870s, when European settlers and sport hunters almost brought the huge North American bison to extinction -- is designated as a World Heritage Site by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO).

Crowshoe said pow wows such as Buffalo Days, held each July for the past 10 years, represent a return for many Indians to ancient ways and an attempt to strengthen their community in the face of increasing outside pressures.
LOST TO ALCOHOL, WHITE MAN'S INFLUENCE

"A lot of our young people have been lost to alcohol and what you would call these white man influences. Our children don't know how to handle them," she said. "We have been taught our ways, traditions, customs from our elders, and it's up to us to hang on to these customs and traditions and pass them on to our younger children."

The customs have spread beyond North America. Conspicuous among Indians readying the site for the evening's spectacle was Frank Winiarz, a 30-year-old German from Berlin who had lived on the Peigan Reserve for a month. Winiarz, a house renovator who was attired in homemade buckskin clothes, is one of thousands of Germans who have embraced Indian customs and spirituality in an attempt to get back to the land.

"For many in Germany, they are named American Indian hobbyists -- for some guys this is a hobby. It is no more a hobby for me, but a second life," Winiarz said as a group of young Indians strode past, one wearing the jersey of Chicago Bulls basketball star Scottie Pippen.

The idea of German hobbyists was viewed by most at the pow wow as a curiousity. But the spread of ancient customs beyond the reservations was seen as positive amid social ills and tension pitting the tribes against Canada's majority population and its government.

That tension, over such issues as land claims and the right to self-government, has exploded into violence in the past few years, with recent armed standoffs occurring at Gustafsen Lake, British Columbia, and Ipperwash, Ontario.

"One of the reasons I come to this pow wow is it is a big tourist attraction," Sleigh said before the brightly colored dancers padded their way into the opening ceremonies amid hypnotic drum beats and chanting. "It helps the world or whoever have awareness of the native tradition here in Canada. It's still alive. It's not gone."
